topic: Multitasking is switching, and every switch costs you
subject: psychology

sources.title: Media Multitasking Effects on Cognitive vs. Attitudinal Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis
“Cognitive control in media multitaskers” ten years on: A meta-analysis

facts.claim: Heavy media multitaskers were better able to switch between tasks in the task-switching paradigm than light media multitaskers.
facts.quote: Across 2 experiments, heavy media multitaskers were better able to switch between tasks in the task-switching paradigm.

facts.claim: Heavy media multitaskers are linked to a reduced ability to filter out interference from irrelevant tasks, which makes them perform worse on a test of task-switching ability.
facts.quote: heavy media multitaskers performed worse on a test of task-switching ability, likely due to reduced ability to filter out interference from the irrelevant task set.

facts.claim: Heavy and light media multitaskers showed comparable performance in the dual-task.
facts.quote: Heavy and light media multitaskers showed comparable performance in the dual-task.

facts.claim: Media multitasking has negative effects on cognitive outcomes, but it has positive effects on attitudinal outcomes.
facts.quote: this meta-analysis showed that multitasking has negative effects on cognitive outcomes, whereas it has positive effects on attitudinal (or persuasion-related) outcomes.

facts.claim: The association between media multitasking and cognitive control is small across measurement approaches and cognitive control functions.
facts.quote: Overall, the pooled effect size of the association, across measurement approaches and cognitive control functions, is small.

facts.claim: As task-switching costs rise, groups increasingly evolve division of labor strategies.
facts.quote: Our results demonstrate that as task-switching costs rise, groups increasingly evolve division of labor strategies.

research.angle: While heavy media multitaskers are linked to worse task-switching ability due to interference, they actually show an increased ability to shift between discrete tasks in specific experimental paradigms.
research.verdict: The evidence is mixed, showing that while multitasking can impair cognitive outcomes and increase susceptibility to interference, it is also associated with improved task-switching abilities in certain contexts.
research.caveat: The research shows significant heterogeneity in outcomes, including conflicting results on whether media multitasking improves or impairs task-switching ability.
